video_title_guess: Warriors Stock Report: Steve Kerr Re-Signs, Draft Lottery Results, Future Outlook

quotes.speaker: Anthony Slater
quotes.quote: You go back to that Friday night and I do think it's almost like you can look at the three weeks very separately one, two, three on what it was. I believe that first week was getting away from the grind. There was the exit interviews with players and coaches, but also just like Steve just getting away to think. And then by the start of the second week, you have the most important meeting in my opinion in this whole process, which was the one we reported on a couple days after it happened. It was that Monday, so I think it was about eight, nine, ten days after the elimination, where it's Ham, it's Mike Dunleavy, it's Joe Lacob, two hours, direction of the franchise, what can and can't be done with the roster, philosophy, staffing, Steve's energy level for the job still, like those type of conversations. And I believe leaving that, there was a sense from both sides from what we heard at the time was how positive, you know, both sides took that meeting very positively, Steve then went on a golf trip, but I think leaving that first meeting, there was a sense of like, oh no, they do want to continue this partnership together.
quotes.why_it_matters: This quote details the crucial steps and discussions that led to Steve Kerr's decision to re-sign with the Warriors, highlighting the positive outcome of a key meeting with ownership and management.

quotes.speaker: Anthony Slater
quotes.quote: They're entering now the transaction season in the NBA and clearly convinced Steve and I think have convinced themselves that while I would probably call it a little bit of a half-measure, they can re-tweak the roster to a degree that there's a more competitive next season. I don't think there's any false hope that they're going to leap into contender status. I think they're going into the summer of the belief that they can do some stuff that keeps them in that mid-tier mix and we're talking top side of that like a five, six probably in the West. And if it's the play-in number one, but also number two, it is a half-measure, right? Because they're not ready to hit eject on a rebuild. And I think part of that calculus is, we know what the lottery odds and the rules are going, it's a, is it really that bad anymore to be, there's not so much more value now of being the 20th best team and the 28th best team in the league.
quotes.why_it_matters: Anthony Slater describes the Warriors' realistic ambition for next season as a "half-measure" to remain competitive (aiming for a 5-6 seed) without fully rebuilding, influenced by new lottery rules that diminish the value of extreme tanking.

quotes.speaker: Tim Bontemps
quotes.quote: Let's just look at the West. Now, setting aside all the ifs you just said, but let's assume there's a realistic summer. They sign some players to try to fill in on the gaps on the wing while Jimmy is rehabbing and most of Moody's not going to play, but Jimmy probably will play for a good chunk of next year. Let's assume that. Let's assume they draft somebody who's an okay pick at 11. Let's even say they get Cedric Ceballos, who is a nice player. I, you know, got a chance to be a very good player, but this year is not, you know, he's like going to maybe play some rotation minutes on the wing, he's not going to come in and be, you know, Conk and Apple, right? Or whatever, Cooper Flag. I only say that to say, yes, I think they're in, they're probably going to be in the mix with Phoenix and Portland and the Clippers again. And we'll see what Dallas does if Kyrie comes back, if they try to be aggressive and getting better, Dallas could be in that mix too. Their ceiling to me is probably eight, maybe seven.
quotes.why_it_matters: Tim Bontemps outlines a realistic ceiling for the Warriors next season, suggesting they'll be in the mix with mid-tier Western Conference teams like Phoenix, Portland, and the Clippers, with their ceiling likely being the 7th or 8th seed.

quotes.speaker: Tim Bontemps
quotes.quote: Are the, the Warriors have any chance to be better than Oklahoma City? The answer is no, right? San Antonio, no. Denver, we would say no, right? Barring a Nikola Jokic departure. Uh, yeah, Minnesota, no. Do we think they could be better than Houston? I would say no. I would say no, but like, why that's a wacky situation. I, it's a wacky situation, but I don't think they're going to be better than Houston. Are they going to be better than the Lakers? I would say no. Realistically, you would assume if they have Luka and Austin Reeves plus whatever, that's probably going to be better than the Warriors with injured players, right? Minnesota, I they're not going to be better than Minnesota. So that's six teams, right? Are they going to be better than Phoenix? That I think's a reasonable question. Well, the other team that I think I would say right now, and this is probably going to freak Warriors fans out, I would say it's definitively going to be better than the Warriors next season is Utah. Yeah, I think Utah's going to be really good. Like, obviously they got the second pick in the draft. They're going to have Walker Kessler and Jaren Jackson and Lauri Markkanen, Keyonte George had a really good year. They've, they've got good depth pieces, they can add more to the roster. I, I think they're going to be a top six or seven team also next year.
quotes.why_it_matters: Tim Bontemps assesses the Warriors' standing against other Western Conference teams, concluding they will likely be worse than several top teams and surprisingly suggests Utah will "definitively" be better next season.

quotes.speaker: Anthony Slater
quotes.quote: One of the most important things for this franchise over the next two to three years, I believe is like guiding out the Steph Curry era like in a very amicable way, not bristling with him at the end, certainly not allowing him to be on another franchise. And part of that is like Steve Kerr, you know, like Steve Kerr guiding that is important. And that's, I think in a lot of ways why he's back. Even if there isn't the contending upside, there's also no longer as the heavy downside of being a play-in, you know, because you still might get a top five pick just, you might just run into one in that bracket. So it's kind of, maybe you would say it's a half-measure, a quiet rebuild to a degree, but it's almost because of situation that we talk about all year, it's kind of what has to be done.
quotes.why_it_matters: Anthony Slater emphasizes that Steve Kerr's return is crucial for the Warriors to "amicably" guide the final years of the Steph Curry era, even if it means a "half-measure" approach to competitiveness rather than a full rebuild.

quotes.speaker: Anthony Slater
quotes.quote: Too far ahead because I mean there's so much we don't know, right? Next year could just, you know, be a disaster, whatever and like, you know, it just makes more sense to to hit eject on a rebuild. Steph Curry could age so gracefully and healthily that he's still playing at 41, 42, right? You know, especially with his shot. And if he decides he wants that, I'm not sure Steve Kerr's ready to go, oh sure Steph, if you got five more years, I got five more years, you know, right, right. So this is just, hey, let's, let's, you know, two years was important, I think for the franchise to get him back on two years as we talked about, right? That was part of the negotiation here, was was the years and they did that, they got two and I think it, it pledges Steve to the the final chapter of Steph Curry's career, but again, I don't think we know for sure, like Steph Curry at this point does not know his end date and I think Steve's is more likelier to be earlier, if if you know what I mean.
quotes.why_it_matters: Anthony Slater explains that Steve Kerr's two-year contract extension was a strategic move to align him with the "final chapter" of Steph Curry's career, but acknowledges that their retirement timelines might not perfectly coincide.

quotes.speaker: Tim Bontemps
quotes.quote: Mike Dunleavy's had a pretty good track record so far as a drafter. If you go look back as we've talked about, I mean, the fact that he has gotten three different players in the 50s to be contributing rotation players, not that any of those guys are complete game-changer players, but Quinton Post and Will Richard and Trayce Jackson-Davis, obviously now in Toronto. But the fact that they drafted three guys in the 50s that have become rotation players for them at different points is a real feather in Mike's Mike Dunleavy's cap. Brandin Podziemski at 19 was a nice pick. Like they, they've done a nice job filling out the Gui Santos was a, a guy that they, they got as an undrafted, or no, he was a, he was in the 50s too, right?
quotes.why_it_matters: Tim Bontemps highlights Mike Dunleavy's strong drafting record, particularly his ability to find contributing rotation players late in the second round, which bodes well for the Warriors' upcoming 11th pick.

quotes.speaker: Anthony Slater
quotes.quote: They spent a lot of the college year scouting, you know, every time I'd go into a city, they'd be, you know, playing in Houston and the Houston Cougars are down the road and a couple of, you know, Chuck Hayes and Mike could go down and watch that game and see Flemings and some of the other guys, I think they're playing Baylor that night. There was a lot of that going on. Like they knew they were going to have in a deep draft, which by the way, loaded with like American college players, right? That's, that's the draft this year. They, they did a lot of leg work. Larry Harris, who you saw at the lottery, heavily involved in that. And they're at the combine this week. I assume they're going to just kind of rotate in a bunch of guys in that potential 11 range to the facility over the next month and decide how much they value the 11th pick and who they like there. They'll make their big board. And then also, I think they're going to look at trades.
quotes.why_it_matters: Anthony Slater details the Warriors' extensive scouting leading up to the draft, indicating they will thoroughly evaluate prospects at pick 11, but also suggests they are open to trading the pick if they don't find a player they "love" in that range.

quotes.speaker: Anthony Slater
quotes.quote: The Giannis domino, I think matters league-wide, not even just like with where Giannis might play next year, but you know, just oftentimes a seismic trade like that has reverberations for several rosters really. And that, I mean, Utah, maybe, but that seems like the first domino of like the, the off-season beyond the draft, I guess I should say.
quotes.why_it_matters: Anthony Slater identifies the potential Giannis Antetokounmpo trade as a major "domino" that could trigger significant league-wide roster changes beyond just the teams directly involved, impacting the Warriors' offseason.

quotes.speaker: Anthony Slater
quotes.quote: Draymond's future, obviously he has the player option to to decide whether to pick up or not. And from what I've gathered and reported, like the Warriors' willingness to do a, you know, decline and extend type scenario with Draymond would depend on like how much immediate benefit they'd get from lowering that first year salary number. If if, you know, if they believe going from 27 to whatever it would be, 18, 19, 20 in that first year would help them go get a guy for a mid-level or whatever, then that's a conversation they'd be willing to have. But also we could be getting towards that option date and it just becomes clear like he's just going to pick it up, you know, and then he's on a $27 million expiring. That also becomes a potential trade tool in some of the trade we're talking about, but trading Draymond Green comes with its own complications.
quotes.why_it_matters: Anthony Slater breaks down Draymond Green's player option decision, explaining that the Warriors' willingness to offer a "decline and extend" deal hinges on whether a lower first-year salary would significantly help them acquire other talent, while also noting the complexities of trading Green.
